cite: Barchet et al. 2024, TenseMusic: an automatic prediction model for musical tension, PLOS ONE
read: full methods, results, limitations via page fetch
corpus: 38 Western classical pieces, 60-90 s, 24 analysed listeners

findings.claim: Each tension feature needed its own attentional and memory window. Different aspects of the same property have different memory lengths.
findings.limit: Classical music only. Not evidence for dance music or room-microphone audio.

findings.claim: Predicted tension correlated with listener ratings at about r = .6 on held-out pieces.
findings.limit: Very uneven across pieces. 8 pieces low or non-significant. Percussion-heavy pieces degraded feature extraction. Authors say applies mainly to Western tonal and atonal classical.

findings.claim: Six audio features: loudness (Zwicker), onset frequency (spectral-flux onsets), tempo (cyclic tempogram), pitch height (polyphonic pitch net), tonal tension (spiral array from transcribed MIDI), roughness (Daniel and Weber). Z-scored, smoothed, 10 Hz.
findings.limit: Loudness, roughness and tonal tension use heavy offline algorithms. Cost on a microcontroller not assessed.

cite: Yadati, Larson, Liem, Hanjalic 2014, Detecting drops in electronic dance music, ISMIR
corpus: SoundCloud EDM tracks with expert and timed-comment drop labels

findings.claim: Community definition: a drop is a moment of emotional release that follows a build and re-introduces the full bassline. No precise recipe. Tracks may contain several. Variability of realisations makes detection hard.

Two stages, offline. Stage 1 segments the track on chroma novelty (12 pitch classes, 209 ms window, 139 ms hop). Stage 2 classifies segment boundaries with a linear SVM on spectrogram statistics, 13 MFCCs and rhythm-pattern features from a fixed window around each boundary.
findings.limit: Whole-track offline, looks ahead. Single platform. Not causal.

findings.claim: A change of rhythm at the drop moment was treated as an informative cue, and the build is visible in the spectrogram before the drop.

cite: Solberg 2014, Waiting for the Bass to Drop, Dancecult
read: abstract plus analysis sections of the PDF
corpus: descriptive analysis of two EDM tracks, spectrograms, expectancy theory. No listener data.

findings.claim: Build-up and drop tension is produced by five documented techniques, and several are not loudness rises.

techniques: drum roll effect (progressively shorter note values)
removal and reintroduction of bass and bass drum
contrasting ambient breakdown before the build

findings.limit: Two tracks and theory. Descriptive, not tested on listeners.

findings.claim: EDM builds layer by layer, elements introduced or removed on 2, 4, 8, 16 or 32 bar boundaries. Groove grows in textural density rather than length.

cite: Juslin and Laukka 2003, Communication of emotions in vocal expression and music performance, Psychological Bulletin
read: cue table only (of a 45-page review of 104 vocal and 41 music-performance studies)
corpus: review, mostly performer-intended emotion, Western, controlled recordings

findings.claim: Discrete emotions have characteristic cue patterns shared between voice and music performance.

music_performance.anger: fast tempo, high sound level, high sound-level variability, high high-frequency energy
music_performance.happiness: fast tempo, medium to high sound level
music_performance.sadness: slow tempo, low sound level, low high-frequency energy
music_performance.tenderness: slow tempo, low sound level, low level variability
music_performance.fear: mixed: mostly low sound level, high level variability

data.note: Compiled from the count-coded table, only the tempo, sound level, level variability and high-frequency energy rows were read. Articulation, mode and pitch rows were not.

findings.limit: Partial account. Cue patterns overlap between emotions. Does not say harmony or tonality contribute independently.

cite: Witek et al. 2014, Syncopation, body-movement and pleasure in groove music, PLOS ONE
read: design and findings as summarised on the article page

findings.claim: Desire to move and pleasure are an inverted U of syncopation degree. Medium syncopation is highest.
findings.limit: Isolated synthetic drum breaks, ratings only, not polyphonic music, not motor synchronisation.

findings.claim: Dancing experience affected ratings. Formal training and groove familiarity mostly did not.

cite: Nieto et al. 2020, Audio-based music structure analysis: current trends, open challenges, and applications, TISMIR

findings.claim: Listeners disagree about structure even in Western popular music. An annotation is ambiguous because it mixes several similarity dimensions. Structure is hierarchical, with few methods exploiting the depth.
Boundary detection reaches roughly 60-70% F1 at 3 s tolerance against a human ceiling estimated near 90%. Multiple annotations per track are recommended.
It remains to be seen how segments could be labelled in real-time causal use.
findings.limit: Stated as an open gap. No causal method was found in what was read.

cite: Muller, Fundamentals of Music Processing, chapter 4 (music structure analysis), online notebook

findings.claim: Structure analysis rests on homogeneity (a stretch stays alike), repetition (sections recur) and novelty (character changes), built on self-similarity matrices and novelty curves. Harmonic, timbral and rhythmic features give different segmentations. Raw matrices need smoothing and tuning.

A standard toolkit groups descriptors as low-level (spectral, loudness, MFCC, bark bands), rhythm (beats, bpm, onset rate, danceability), tonal (key, HPCP chroma, chords) and classifier-derived high-level. Useful as a checklist of evidence sources.
